concepts.decision: Apply language/architecture-aware standards, threat-informed review, tests, exception governance, and production feedback.
concepts.definition: Repeatable coding and review practices that prevent or reduce known weakness classes while preserving intended behavior under normal, invalid, and hostile conditions.
concepts.failureExample: A one-time secure-coding course without review and testing does not control a new authorization defect.
concepts.label: Secure Coding

concepts.decision: Validate syntactic and semantic rules as close as practical to receipt; allowlist expected values and treat client validation as UX, not security.
concepts.definition: Server-side enforcement that untrusted data has permitted type, structure, length, range, encoding, and business meaning before use.
concepts.failureExample: A client-side-only price check can be bypassed by a crafted request.
concepts.label: Input Validation

concepts.decision: Encode when emitting data into its target context and use suitable rendering APIs; do not rely on input filters to predict future contexts.
concepts.definition: Transforming data for the exact output interpreter/context so untrusted content is displayed as data rather than executed as markup, script, URL, or other code.
concepts.failureExample: HTML encoding text placed inside a JavaScript context can still create executable behavior.
concepts.label: Output Encoding

concepts.decision: Return minimal user-facing errors, log protected diagnostic context, and define safe rollback/failure behavior.
concepts.definition: Safe handling of expected and unexpected failures that preserves availability and diagnosability without exposing internal details or secrets.
concepts.failureExample: An API stack trace can disclose schema, paths, or tokens that help an attacker.
concepts.label: Error Handling

concepts.decision: Choose strong, managed authentication appropriate to the actor and protect credential/token lifecycle; authentication alone does not grant object access.
concepts.definition: Verification of the identity or credential presented by a user, service, or device.
concepts.failureExample: A valid customer token may still be used to request another customer’s invoice.
concepts.label: Authentication

concepts.decision: Check server-side at each sensitive action/object boundary using least privilege and deny-by-default behavior.
concepts.definition: Enforcement of whether an authenticated principal may perform a requested action on a specific object or resource in the current context.
concepts.failureExample: Checking only that a token is valid enables insecure direct object access.
concepts.label: Authorization

concepts.decision: Model API abuse paths and test valid/invalid callers, object IDs, token reuse, rate behavior, and response data.
concepts.definition: Protection of programmatic interfaces through identity, object/action authorization, input/schema validation, rate/replay controls, data minimization, versioning, safe errors, and observability.
concepts.failureExample: An authenticated API with no object-level authorization can expose every tenant’s data.
concepts.label: API Security

concepts.decision: Use managed scoped storage/retrieval, rotation, revocation, redaction, and separate environment identities; never hardcode or expose them in errors/logs.
concepts.definition: Credentials, keys, tokens, connection strings, and sensitive values whose disclosure or misuse grants access or weakens controls.
concepts.failureExample: A database password embedded in client code can be extracted and used outside the intended application.
concepts.label: Secrets

concepts.decision: Combine parameterized data access with object/row authorization, least privilege, auditing and appropriate retention/minimization.
concepts.definition: Protection of transactional and analytical data, queries, service identities and permitted data use.
concepts.failureExample: A parameterized query is injection-safe but exposes another customer’s records because authorization was omitted.
concepts.label: Database Data Warehouse Security

concepts.decision: Validate inputs server-side, enforce authorization on protected operations, and encode output for the actual output context.
concepts.definition: The browser, service, session and data-processing contexts through which a web application accepts input and produces output.
concepts.failureExample: A stored comment becomes script because the dashboard renders it as executable markup.
concepts.label: Web Application Environment

misconceptions.claim: A hidden API endpoint is protected because users cannot see it.
misconceptions.correction: Discovery, direct requests, alternate clients, and compromised credentials require explicit authentication and authorization.

outcome: Choose coding practices that prevent common source, API, authentication, authorization, and error-handling weaknesses.

sections.body: Validate inputs against an allowlist and expected type, length, range, and encoding; use context-appropriate output encoding; avoid unsafe interpretation and injection; fail safely; protect error and log content; and make resource and authorization checks explicit. Use standards and peer review to make these rules repeatable.
keyPoints: Validation and output encoding solve different boundary problems.
Error messages should aid operators without disclosing secrets or internals.
Authorization must be checked at the server-side object and action boundary.
sections.title: Control inputs, outputs, state, and errors

sections.body: API security includes authentication, authorization, object-level access, replay and rate controls, schema validation, data minimization, versioning, secure defaults, and consistent error behavior. Protect credentials and tokens, define service identity, and test abuse cases rather than only valid requests.
keyPoints: An authenticated caller is not automatically authorized for every object or action.
API contracts need negative, boundary, and abuse-case tests.
Secrets should be handled through managed lifecycle controls, not source literals.
sections.title: Secure API contracts and identities

sections.body: For database and data-warehouse access, separate authorization from query construction; use parameterized interfaces, least-privileged service identities, controlled analytics access, audit, retention and data-minimization rules. For web applications, validate untrusted input server-side, encode output for its exact HTML/attribute/URL/JavaScript context, protect session and transport behavior, and test authenticated and unauthenticated abuse paths.
keyPoints: Parameterization prevents data being interpreted as query structure; it does not decide who may access an object.
Output encoding is context-specific and complements, rather than replaces, validation.
Database/warehouse and web controls need tests that use realistic roles and data flows.
sections.title: Secure data access and web contexts explicitly
